To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) synaptically induced changes in input conductance are visible from the cell soma; (2) the observed conductance change due to a synaptic input does not depend on its reversal potential; and (3) for an idealized passive dendritic tree, the change in somatic input resistance decays exponentially with the distance from the synapse to the recording site.

(1) synaptic conductance changes are not necessarily visible from the cell soma and (2) in a large class of neurons (e.g., cortical pyramidal neurons) the increase in somatic conductance due to a synaptically induced change is clearly visible from electrodes impaling the soma.

(1) the change in input (somatic) resistance is less than the sum over all synaptic inputs and does not depend on synaptic reversal potential and (2) the change in somatic input resistance due to activity of inhibitory basket cells of morphologically identified pyramids is clearly visible from intracellular electrodes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the visibility of synaptic conductance changes in intracellular recordings from cortical neurons and the consequences of such changes for models of cortical function.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the change in the input conductance at the soma due to synaptic activity can be estimated from the change in the membrane potential at the soma, and this estimate is not affected by the location of the synapse or the reversal potential of the synaptic input.
